docs.title: exo-v2v
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.3.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

exo-v2v moves a running VMware vSphere virtual machine to an Exoscale Compute instance. The VM keeps running while its disks are copied; it is stopped only for the final cutover, which took 2 to 9 minutes in our tests, whatever the size of the disks.

  • Replicate while the VM runs. The VM's disks are copied straight to the disks of the target instance, then kept in sync with VMware Changed Block Tracking: each cycle copies only what changed.
  • Cut over. The VM is shut down, the last changes are copied, the guest is converted for KVM on the target instance itself, and the instance boots the migrated system from its own disks.

No VDDK, no vSphere plugin, no agent inside the guest, no staging storage.

docs.title: What it handles
docs.text: Area Supported Guests Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL family) and Windows Server 2022/2025, BIOS or UEFI, Secure Boot, vTPM (details) Disks Several VMDKs per VM on SCSI, SATA or NVMe controllers; the system disk is found from the boot order or VMware Tools; up to 5 data disks as Block Storage volumes VMDK chains VMs running on snapshot deltas, at any depth. Snapshots may be taken, deleted or reverted during replication: a revert makes the next cycle copy the allocated areas again Disks that change A disk grown during replication is followed (its volume is resized; a grown system disk resets the target instance); a disk added is replicated to a new volume LVM Volume groups spread over several disks. A disk that extends the system disk's volume group is carried inside the root disk; logical volumes on data disks are rebuilt for 4 KiB sectors when their filesystem needs it, with the same UUIDs Filesystems ext, XFS (including 512-byte-sector XFS, the RHEL default on VMware), NTFS, swap; partition tables GPT and MBR Replication Changed Block Tracking, VDDK-free, through a replication appliance in vSphere; several migrations at once from one appliance Applications A group of VMs (load balancer, application servers, databases) replicated together and cut over in one window: stopped front to back, converted in parallel, started back to front with health checks, rolled back as a whole Networks Each vSphere port group maps to the public interface or an Exoscale private network; VMs keep their private addresses, the guest's network configuration follows the new NICs Status page A read-only web page on the appliance with every migration and group Not supported Independent disks, raw device mappings, encrypted disks, Windows dynamic disks and Storage Spaces as data disks (limitations)

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
On the replication appliance (a Linux VM in the same vSphere environment, with Python 3.10 or later and the exo CLI):

pipx install https://github.com/retrack/exo-v2v/releases/download/v0.3.0/exo_v2v-0.3.0-py3-none-any.whl
exo config                          # Exoscale credentials for the exo CLI
export VSPHERE_HOST=vcenter.example VSPHERE_USER=migration@vsphere.local VSPHERE_PASSWORD=…

docs.title: Migrate a VM
docs.text:
exo-v2v plan    web01 --vm web01 --zone ch-gva-2 --security-group web
exo-v2v create  web01                   # target instance and volumes
sudo -E exo-v2v sync web01              # first cycle: full copy, the VM keeps running
sudo -E exo-v2v sync web01 --every 900  # keep it fresh until the maintenance window
sudo -E exo-v2v cutover web01           # downtime starts here
exo-v2v cleanup web01                   # after you validated the workload

plan prints everything it will do and refuses unsupported VMs; nothing is created before create. Every step can be repeated or resumed, and exo-v2v rollback powers the source VM back on until cleanup.

docs.title: Move an application
docs.text:
exo-v2v group discover shop --vm lb01 --vm app01 --vm app02 --vm db01 --zone ch-gva-2
exo-v2v group plan    shop -f shop.yaml     # after setting tiers, health checks, security groups
exo-v2v group create  shop                  # private networks, anti-affinity, receivers
sudo -E exo-v2v group sync shop --every 900
sudo -E exo-v2v group cutover shop          # one window for the whole application

See Moving an application. sudo -E exo-v2v web shows every migration and group on a read-only page.

docs.title: Why the target instance is the receiver
docs.text:
There is no staging copy: the bytes land on the disks that will run the workload. The instance keeps its boot mode (and Secure Boot / TPM, set with --secureboot / --tpm from the source's settings) for life, so it is created in the source's firmware mode. Its receiver system must run from RAM, so that /dev/vda can be overwritten. There are two ways to get there.

Receiver template (plan --receiver-template, see receiver-templates.md). The template's disk holds a BIOS boot partition and an EFI system partition; Canonical-signed shim and GRUB load the kernel and a ~220 MB initramfs that is the root filesystem (mmdebstrap Ubuntu 24.04 with virt-v2v, libguestfs, QEMU, filesystem tools). At boot, v2v-userdata-key installs the SSH key from the instance user-data for user v2v, v2v-hostkeys generates host keys, and on the Windows variant v2v-winsupport copies virtio-win and rhsrvany from the EFI partition into RAM (kept out of the initramfs: GRUB loading 400+ MB through firmware I/O did not always finish). create waits for SSH before attaching volumes (a disk hot-plugged while the firmware loads the initramfs can hang the boot), then streams the agent and restarts v2v-agent.

Stock template (default). The instance is created from Debian 13 (BIOS) or Ubuntu 24.04 (UEFI). Cloud-init only installs the migration's SSH key; exo-v2v create then streams the agent payload (tar.gz) over SSH and starts the bootstrap detached (Exoscale caps user-data at 32 KiB base64, which the payload outgrew). The bootstrap waits for cloud-init and the dpkg lock, installs virt-v2v/libguestfs/xfsprogs, copies the running OS into a RAM filesystem, packs it as an initramfs and kexecs into it with the same kernel. From then on nothing uses /dev/vda or the volumes: the agent exports them over NBD on 127.0.0.1 only.

Consequence (documented limit): if the receiver reboots during the sync window, it boots the half-written disk. exo-v2v detects a receiver that left its RAM root and asks for recreation; a restarted agent (lost /meta) triggers a full cycle automatically.

docs.title: Data path
docs.text:
appliance                                              receiver (RAM root)
vsphere.sync ─ NBD client ─ ssh -L ─ (TCP 22) ─ sshd ─ nbdserve 127.0.0.1:10809 ─ /dev/vdX
cli          ─ HTTP       ─ ssh -L ─ (TCP 22) ─ sshd ─ agent API 127.0.0.1:8787
  • Authentication: a per-migration ed25519 key, injected through cloud-init user-data; a per-migration security group opens TCP 22 to the appliance's egress address only. No other port is exposed during the sync window.
  • NBD: fixed-newstyle, simple replies, 32 MiB max payload, WRITE_ZEROES implemented with BLKZEROOUT (offloadable) instead of writing zeros.

docs.title: Replication without VDDK
docs.text:
Per cycle and per disk:

  1. CreateSnapshot (no memory, no quiesce) → the snapshot's disk backing is the frozen base .vmdk + its CBT changeId.
  2. QueryChangedDiskAreas(snapshot, disk, changeId); "*" on the first cycle (allocated areas; the rest is zeroed on the target).
  3. Hot-add: ReconfigVM on the appliance adds the base .vmdk as independent_nonpersistent — the source is opened read-only, appliance writes would go to a throw-away redo log. The block device is located by SCSI target = unit number and size; ranges are read with pread (parallel workers) and written to NBD; zero chunks become WRITE_ZEROES.
  4. Detach (no file operation — never deletes), POST /meta {change_id} on the receiver, RemoveSnapshot.

A VM on a chain of snapshot deltas needs nothing special: the snapshot's backing is the top of the chain, and hot-add opens the whole chain read-only. A changeId that vSphere no longer accepts (a snapshot revert resets CBT: new change-tracking UUID, the old IDs raise FileFault) makes that disk's cycle a copy of its allocated areas ("*"), the rest zeroed.

docs.title: Disks changing between cycles
docs.text:
reconcile_disks compares the VM's disks with the plan before every cycle (and before the cutover's downtime):

  • grown Block Storage disk: detach, update --size (Exoscale resizes detached volumes only), attach, find the device by serial, POST /exports (the NBD server restarts with the new device; the export's change ID is dropped, so the next cycle copies it whole);
  • grown system disk or folded disk beyond the root disk: the receiver is rebuilt with reset-instance (stop, re-image the root disk from the template at the new size, start, agent again). Volumes are detached first and their change IDs saved and restored, so only the root disk is copied again. The state records rebuild_pending until it completes: an interrupted rebuild is resumed by the next sync/cutover;
  • new disk: a new volume and export;
  • removed disk: stop.

The agent maps volumes to exports by virtio serial (Exoscale: the volume ID's first 20 characters, volumes.json in the payload), not by device order.

docs.title: Folded disks
docs.text:
A disk listed in folds.json (export, byte offset, size) is a region of the root disk after the system disk (1 MiB aligned, 1 MiB kept free at the end for a backup GPT). The agent exports it through a loop device (--direct-io). At /convert, before virt-v2v, the loop devices are released and guestfix.fold adds the region's partitions (or the whole region when it has no table) to the root disk's MBR or GPT, keeping the partition types and GPT GUIDs. virt-v2v then sees the guest's volume groups complete, on 512-byte sectors.

Why not the datastore HTTP file service: hostd needs an exclusive lock to serve *-flat.vmdk; a running VM's base disk is locked (Failed to lock file, HTTP 500). --transport http remains for powered-off VMs.

Robustness: a host-wide flock serializes hot-add attach and detach on one appliance (concurrent migrations otherwise collide in vSphere with TaskInProgress, and attach retries it); a per-migration lock forbids two writers; at start the sweep removes this source VM's leftover v2v-sync-* snapshots and hot-added disks (never other VMs'); vSphere task methods wait for the VM to be idle and retry TaskInProgress. CBT is enabled VM-wide and per disk (scsiX:Y.ctkEnabled) with a snapshot stun cycle; a disk whose CBT is inactive is copied whole for that cycle.

The changeId is stored on the receiver (RAM), not on the appliance: it is only valid together with the exact bytes on the receiver's disks.

docs.title: Cutover and conversion
docs.text:
1. Final cycle after guest shutdown (Tools) / power-off.
  2. POST /convert: virt-v2v-in-place -i disk /dev/vda /dev/vdb … with nested KVM (LIBGUESTFS_BACKEND=direct); Windows gets VIRTIO_WIN + rhsrvany (staged by win-support.sh, or built into the Windows receiver template).
  3. guestfix.adapt on each data volume, LVM analysis across all disks (lvm_report), guestfix.netfix on the root disk. On Windows, netfix instead queues a script in virt-v2v's firstboot framework that registers a SYSTEM scheduled task: it sets the SAN policy to OnlineAll and onlines the data disks, retries until the storage services answer, and deletes itself. The script re-queues itself first, because firstboot can run it while Windows is shutting down for a driver reboot.
  4. POST /relayout {"spares": {export: device}} per relayout group (one volume, or the volumes a volume group spans), onto spare volumes the CLI creates and attaches; the CLI then detaches the originals (kept, labelled exo-v2v-rollback). Groups run smallest first; each needs a free volume slot per member.
  5. stop → scale (conversion needs ≥ 8 GiB RAM: receivers run as standard.large at least) → start → attach the user's security groups → wait for 22/3389.

docs.title: 4Kn Block Storage
docs.text:
Exoscale volumes expose 4096-byte logical sectors; the instance root disk exposes 512. VMware disks are 512. guestfix:

  • analyze: partition table kind and sector unit (GPT header at LBA 1 of 512 or 4096; for MBR the unit is inferred from where a filesystem signature sits — MBR does not record it), filesystems per partition: XFS sectsz, ext block size, NTFS bytes/sector, LVM PV, swap.
  • adapt: rewrite GPT (pMBR, header, entries, backup, CRC32s) or MBR in 4K units in place; requires 4 KiB-aligned partitions and ≥ 1 MiB slack at the end of the volume (the CLI provisions volumes with that slack).
  • NTFS: the boot sector's bytes-per-sector (and the derived geometry) is rewritten for 4096 in place (ntfs_rebps); clusters must be ≥ 4 KiB. The original boot sector is kept for revert.
  • relayout: copy table region + tail, adapt the spare, block-copy compatible partitions, recreate XFS-512 / ext-1K with 4K geometry and the same UUID/label, fill with xfsdump | xfsrestore (XFS) or rsync -aAXHS, reading the source through a read-only losetup --sector-size 512 view.
  • LVM (lvmlayout.py): the receiver never activates the guest's volume groups. It reads the PV labels, PV headers and the current text metadata from the disks, maps each logical volume to byte ranges, and probes the filesystem at its start. A linear or striped LV with a 512-only filesystem on 4Kn volumes is rebuilt: the PV headers and metadata areas, and the extents of the other LVs, are copied byte for byte onto the spares (same PV/VG/LV UUIDs, same extents); the LV is assembled twice with dmsetup (old: over read-only 512-sector loop views of the sources; new: over the spares) and rebuild_fs runs between the two. A volume group with a PV on the system disk is not rebuilt: its other disks must be folded.
  • Windows dynamic disks / Storage Spaces (GPT partition types for LDM metadata and data, MBR type 0x42, Storage Spaces): their own metadata counts 512-byte sectors; they are left untouched and reported.

docs.title: Network fix-up
docs.text:
virt-v2v converts drivers but not interface naming. v2v-netfix.service (oneshot, Before=network-pre.target, every boot, idempotent) maps configured names that no longer exist to NICs that are not configured, in order, across ifupdown, netplan, NetworkManager keyfiles and ifcfg; turns allow-hotplug into auto (the hotplug event may have fired before the fix); removes VMware OUI MAC pins and persistent-net rules; runs netplan generate; falls back to DHCP on the first NIC. Log: /var/log/v2v-netfix.log.

With a plan that maps NICs (groups), POST /convert {"netmap": [...]} carries the instance's NICs by MAC (exo x get-instance: the CLI's instance show has no MACs), public first. The receiver writes /etc/v2v-netfix.map (MAC static ADDR/LEN nogw or MAC dhcp) and the service applies it first: the configuration holding each static address is renamed to the NIC with that MAC (in two phases through temporary names, so eth0 → eth1 swaps work), its gateway is removed (gateway, gateway4, default routes, GATEWAY= with DEFROUTE=no, NetworkManager never-default=true), and a DHCP configuration is written in the guest's own stack for a mapped NIC left without one. A profile bound only by MAC gets an interface-name. Windows: a first-boot scheduled task (same pattern as the disk task) sets the addresses with New-NetIPAddress on the adapters with those MACs.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
group plan builds each member's plan (plan.build with the NIC map from plan.network_map) and stores groups/NAME/group.json next to the member states (GROUP-VM, state.data["group"]). group create makes the private networks (managed, range = the subnet minus the top address), anti-affinity groups (create-time only on Exoscale, so they go into instance create) and security groups, then runs create per member; create attaches the private networks with --ip (static leases) and records the NIC MACs.

Members' sync and cutover run as child processes (python -m exo_v2v ... --in-group) in their own sessions, each writing its log file: a member keeps going if the group process dies, and a group command run again finds it by the pid in the member's lock file. The per-VM cutover is split into recorded steps (cutover_steps: down_at, source_off, final_cycle, convert_started, converted, flushed, stopped, scaled, started) so that it resumes anywhere; cutover --no-start stops after the flush. The group cutover is a state machine in group.json (preflight, warm, pre_hook, stop_started, tierN_off, converted, tierN_up, post_hook): it starts the member cutovers tier by tier from the front, waits for each tier's source_off before shutting down the next, waits for every conversion, stops and scales all instances, then starts tier by tier from the back with health checks. group rollback stops the converted instances front first and calls the per-VM rollback back end first; a member whose conversion had not started keeps its receiver and returns to syncing.

docs.title: Web status page
docs.text: exo-v2v web is a ThreadingHTTPServer serving web.html (inline CSS and JavaScript, no external requests) and a JSON API over the state files. It answers GET/HEAD only, never opens a state file for writing and never takes a lock: running commands are found from the pid each lock file records (checked against /proc/PID/cmdline). Member logs are served by member name only, never by a path from the URL. Off loopback it requires a token (bearer header or an HTTP-only cookie set by /login).

docs.title: exo-v2v operations runbook
docs.text: Experimental. exo-v2v 0.3.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

docs.title: 1. Replication appliance (once per vSphere environment)
docs.text:
A small Linux VM on a host that sees the source datastores (one appliance can serve several migrations; hot-adds are serialized on it):

  • Ubuntu 24.04 / Debian 12+, 2 vCPU, 4 GiB RAM, 20 GB disk, paravirtual SCSI controller (free units are used for hot-added disks; add a second pvscsi controller if you run many migrations in parallel).
  • Network: TCP 443 to vCenter/ESXi, TCP 22 to the Exoscale zone(s).
  • Software: python3 -m pip install exo_v2v-*.whl (or pipx), the exo CLI configured with an API key limited to the compute service.
  • Run sync/cutover as root (sudo -E, so VSPHERE_* / EXOSCALE_* pass).

vSphere permissions for the migration account: on the source VMs VirtualMachine.State.CreateSnapshot/RemoveSnapshot, VirtualMachine.Config.ChangeTracking, VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOff/PowerOn (cutover/rollback), VirtualMachine.Provisioning.DiskRandomRead; on the appliance VM VirtualMachine.Config.AddExistingDisk/RemoveDisk; Datastore.FileManagement (read).

docs.title: 2. A migration, end to end
docs.text:
Step Command Duration Source VM Plan exo-v2v plan NAME --vm VM --zone Z [--instance-type T] [--security-group SG] [--receiver-template TPL] seconds untouched Receiver exo-v2v create NAME ~1 min with a receiver template, 5–15 min without untouched Initial copy sudo -E exo-v2v sync NAME allocated data / throughput running (snapshot during the cycle) Keep fresh sudo -E exo-v2v sync NAME --every 900 per cycle: changes since last cycle running Cutover sudo -E exo-v2v cutover NAME final delta + convert (2–5 min) + relayout (if any) + boot shut down Validate test the application on the instance off Finish exo-v2v cleanup NAME [--delete-rollback-volumes] off (keep it until you are sure)

Downtime ≈ shutdown + last delta + conversion + boot. Run a sync cycle shortly before the cutover so that the final delta is small.

exo-v2v status [-v] [NAME] shows the phase, the last cycle and its age.

docs.title: An application (group)
docs.text:
Step Command Source VMs Draft exo-v2v group discover NAME --vm A --vm B ... --zone Z then edit NAME.yaml untouched Plan exo-v2v group plan NAME -f NAME.yaml untouched Networks + receivers exo-v2v group create NAME untouched Copy and keep fresh sudo -E exo-v2v group sync NAME [--every 900] running Window sudo -E exo-v2v group cutover NAME shut down, front to back Follow exo-v2v group status NAME, the web page, ~/.exo-v2v/groups/NAME/logs/VM.log Finish exo-v2v group cleanup NAME off

Before the window: lower the TTL of the DNS names that will move (the load balancer's new address is its receiver's IP, shown by group status), and check that group sync ran recently (cutover.max_sync_age).

docs.title: 3. Rollback
docs.text:
Before cleanup the source VM is intact (only its CBT setting was enabled): exo-v2v rollback NAME powers it back on and stops the Exoscale instance. After a cutover, data written on Exoscale is not copied back.

For a group, exo-v2v group rollback NAME stops the Exoscale instances (front first) and powers the sources on, back end first. Members that were not converted yet keep syncing.

docs.title: 5. Clean-up of Exoscale resources
docs.text: Everything exo-v2v creates carries the label exo-v2v=<NAME>: the instance, its volumes, <volume>-4k relayout volumes and the security group exo-v2v-<NAME>. A group also creates v2v-GROUP-* private networks, anti-affinity groups and the security groups its manifest defines; group cleanup --delete-instances removes them. Rollback copies of relaid volumes additionally carry exo-v2v-rollback=<export>.

docs.title: How exo-v2v works
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.3.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

exo-v2v moves a running VMware vSphere virtual machine to an Exoscale Compute instance. The VM keeps running while its disks are copied. It is stopped only for the final cutover, which took 2 to 9 minutes in our tests, whatever the size of the disks.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
Part Where it runs What it does exo-v2v (CLI) The replication appliance, a small Linux VM you deploy in the same vSphere environment as the VMs to migrate Plans the migration, creates the Exoscale resources, copies the disks, drives the cutover Target instance Your Exoscale zone The instance that will run the migrated VM. During the migration it runs a temporary agent from memory, so its own disks can be overwritten. It starts either from a receiver template that boots straight into memory (about 1 minute) or from a stock Linux template that installs the tools first (5 to 15 minutes) Root disk and Block Storage volumes Attached to the target instance Receive the VM's disks: the system disk becomes the instance's root disk, the others become Block Storage volumes (see The VM's disks)

There is no intermediate copy: the data lands directly on the disks the migrated VM boots from.

docs.title: Replicating while the VM runs
docs.text:
exo-v2v uses VMware Changed Block Tracking (CBT), the mechanism backup products use. Each sync cycle copies only what changed since the previous one.

  1. A short-lived VM snapshot freezes the disks at a point in time.
  2. vSphere reports which areas changed since the last cycle. The first cycle copies every allocated area.
  3. The frozen disk is attached read-only to the appliance (hot-add), together with the snapshot deltas below it when the VM already runs on a chain of snapshots, so the appliance sees the disk exactly as the VM does. It reads the changed areas and writes them to the target instance through an SSH tunnel.
  4. The target instance records the cycle's change ID; the snapshot is deleted.

No VMware software development kit (VDDK) is needed, and nothing is installed inside the VM. Run exo-v2v sync NAME --every 900 to start a cycle every 15 minutes until your maintenance window.

docs.title: The VM's disks
docs.text:
A VM can have several virtual disks (VMDKs), on SCSI, SATA or NVMe controllers, and each disk can be a chain of snapshot deltas. exo-v2v plan maps each of them:

VM disk On Exoscale The system disk The instance's root disk. exo-v2v finds it from the VM's boot order, then from VMware Tools (the disk holding /boot or C:\), then from bios.hddOrder. If none of these answers, plan warns that it guessed; --system-disk sets it. Other disks One Block Storage volume each, up to 5 A disk that shares a filesystem with the system disk, such as a root volume group extended onto a second VMDK (Linux) Carried inside the root disk: replicated into a region after the system disk, then added as a partition of the root disk at cutover. A 4096-byte-sector volume cannot hold part of a volume group whose filesystem only works with 512-byte sectors. plan detects it with VMware Tools; --fold DISK forces it, --no-fold turns it off.

Snapshots and changes during replication:

  • Existing snapshots. A VM that runs on a chain of snapshot deltas is replicated as it is: each cycle reads the disks as the VM sees them. Deleting snapshots during replication is fine. Reverting to a snapshot resets CBT: the next cycle copies the allocated areas of every disk again.
  • A disk grows. The next cycle resizes its Block Storage volume (detach, resize, attach) and copies the disk again. When the system disk, or a disk carried inside it, grows beyond the root disk, the target instance is reset with a bigger root disk and its agent restarted. Its volumes are kept, and only the root disk is copied again.
  • A disk is added. The next cycle creates a volume for it and copies it.
  • A disk is removed. sync stops: plan the migration again.

docs.title: The migration lifecycle
docs.text:
Step Command The source VM Check the VM and size the instance exo-v2v plan Untouched Create the target instance and volumes exo-v2v create Untouched First copy, then keep it fresh exo-v2v sync [--every SECONDS] Running Switch over exo-v2v cutover Shut down: downtime starts Validate, then close the migration exo-v2v cleanup Off, kept until you delete it

Every step can be repeated or resumed after an interruption. Until cleanup, exo-v2v rollback powers the source VM back on and stops the Exoscale instance.

docs.title: What happens at cutover
docs.text:
1. The VM is shut down through VMware Tools (or powered off after a timeout), and the last changes are copied.
  2. The guest is converted for the KVM hypervisor on the target instance itself, with virt-v2v-in-place: virtio drivers, boot loader and initramfs, removal of VMware Tools.
  3. exo-v2v adapts the guest to Exoscale (see below).
  4. The instance restarts from its own disks, is scaled to its final instance type, receives your security groups, and exo-v2v waits until SSH (Linux) or RDP (Windows) answers.

Downtime is the sum of the shutdown, the last delta, the conversion (2 to 5 minutes) and the boot. Run a sync shortly before the cutover so that the last delta is small. Measured values per guest are in Supported operating systems.

docs.title: Adapting the guest to Exoscale
docs.text:
These adjustments are automatic:

Difference What exo-v2v does Network interfaces get new names and MAC addresses A first-boot service maps the old interface names in the network configuration to the new ones, removes VMware MAC pinning, and falls back to DHCP. In a group it follows a map by MAC address: a static address moves to the private network NIC that keeps it, the public interface gets DHCP Block Storage volumes use 4096-byte sectors; VMware disks use 512 Partition tables are rewritten for 4096-byte sectors. NTFS volumes are adapted in place. XFS and ext filesystems that only work with 512-byte sectors are rebuilt on a new volume with the same identifiers, as partitions or as LVM logical volumes (a volume group spread over several volumes is rebuilt across new ones, with the same LVM identifiers). The original volumes are kept as rollback copies Windows keeps new disks offline A first-boot task sets the SAN policy to OnlineAll and brings the data disks online Secure Boot and TPM The instance is created with Secure Boot and a TPM when the source VM has them SELinux guests Files exo-v2v adds are labelled correctly, so no relabelling reboot is needed

docs.title: Applications
docs.text: A group moves several VMs as one application. Each member is an ordinary migration; the group adds a manifest (tiers, networks, health checks, hooks), private networks that keep the VMs' addresses, and a coordinated cutover: the tiers stop front to back, every member converts in parallel, and the tiers start back to front, each after the previous one passes its health checks. group rollback brings the whole application back on VMware.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
• The appliance needs an Exoscale API key limited to Compute (see IAM role) and a vSphere account allowed to snapshot the VMs.
  • Each migration gets its own SSH key and its own security group. That group opens TCP 22 only, and only to the appliance's public address. No other port is exposed during replication.
  • In a group, each member's own security group also opens its health check ports to the appliance only, until cleanup.
  • The data stream runs inside SSH. The agent's disk export and control API listen on the instance's loopback interface only.
  • Snapshots are read through a read-only attachment; exo-v2v never writes to the source VM's disks.

docs.title: Moving an application (groups)
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.3.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

A group moves several VMs that work together, for example a load balancer, a few application servers and a database, as one unit. Every VM is replicated while it runs, like a single migration. The cutover is coordinated: one maintenance window, the VMs stopped and started in a set order, health checks between the steps, and one command to bring the whole application back on VMware if something fails.

docs.title: What a group adds
docs.text:
Feature What it does Order Tiers: tier 1 is the back end (databases), higher tiers are closer to the users. The cutover stops the highest tier first and starts tier 1 first Downtime Each VM's final copy and conversion start as soon as that VM is off, and the conversions run in parallel: the window is close to the slowest member's downtime, not the sum Private addresses A vSphere port group maps to an Exoscale managed private network. Each VM keeps its address there (a static lease), so configurations that name other servers by IP keep working Health checks TCP, HTTP or a command, run from the appliance after each tier starts. The next tier starts only when the checks pass Hooks Commands run on the appliance before the first VM stops and after the last tier is healthy (maintenance page, DNS switch) Placement Anti-affinity groups keep VMs such as the two application servers on different hypervisors Rollback group rollback stops the Exoscale instances and powers the sources on, back end first Resume The cutover records every step. If the appliance or the command stops, group cutover again continues where it stopped

Members are ordinary migrations named GROUP-VM (shop-db01): exo-v2v status and the web status page show them, and their logs are in ~/.exo-v2v/groups/GROUP/logs/.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
exo-v2v group discover shop --vm lb01 --vm app01 --vm app02 --vm db01 --zone ch-gva-2   # draft shop.yaml
vi shop.yaml                                     # tiers, security groups, health checks, hooks
exo-v2v group plan     shop -f shop.yaml         # every member's plan + the cutover runbook
exo-v2v group create   shop                      # private networks, anti-affinity groups, receivers
sudo -E exo-v2v group sync shop                  # a cycle on every member, in parallel
sudo -E exo-v2v group sync shop --every 900      # keep them fresh until the window
sudo -E exo-v2v group cutover shop               # the window
exo-v2v group status   shop
sudo -E exo-v2v group rollback shop              # if needed: back on VMware
exo-v2v group cleanup  shop                      # after validation

group plan checks every VM as plan does, plus the group: every port group mapped, no address used twice, security groups present, instance and private network quotas. Nothing is created before group create.

docs.title: The manifest
docs.text:
group discover writes a draft from vSphere: one network per port group, with the addresses VMware Tools reports. A port group that carries the default route of a VM with several NICs is taken for the front end (the public interface). Check every line.

name: shop
zone: ch-gva-2

defaults:                               # any per-VM key, for every VM
  receiver_template: exo-v2v-linux-legacy
  receiver_template_visibility: private

networks:                               # vSphere port group -> Exoscale
  front:
    source: pg-front
    type: public                        # the instance's public interface (DHCP)
  app:
    source: pg-app
    type: private                       # a managed private network, v2v-shop-app
    cidr: 10.20.0.0/24
    keep_addresses: true                # static leases = the VMs' current addresses

security_groups:                        # created by `group create` when missing
  v2v-shop-web: [tcp/80 0.0.0.0/0, tcp/443 0.0.0.0/0]
  v2v-shop-closed: []                   # no ingress at all

anti_affinity:
  app: [app01, app02]                   # different hypervisors (set at creation)

vms:
  - vm: db01
    tier: 1                             # started first, stopped last
    security_groups: [v2v-shop-closed]
    health: {tcp: 5432}
  - vm: app01
    tier: 2
    security_groups: [v2v-shop-closed]
    health: {http: "http://{public_ip}:8080/health", expect: ok}
  - vm: app02
    tier: 2
    security_groups: [v2v-shop-closed]
    health: {http: "http://{public_ip}:8080/health", expect: ok}
  - vm: lb01
    tier: 3                             # stopped first, started last
    security_groups: [v2v-shop-web]
    health: {http: "http://{public_ip}/", expect: "beats"}
    name: lb01                          # renamed at cleanup (default: v2v-shop-lb01)

hooks:
  pre_cutover: ./maintenance-page.sh on
  post_cutover: ./switch-dns.sh {lb01.public_ip}

cutover:
  parallel: 8                           # member cutovers at a time
  max_window: 30m                       # stop when exceeded
  rollback_on_failure: false            # true: roll back on any failure
  health_timeout: 10m
  max_sync_age: 6h                      # members must have synced this recently
Key Meaning networks.NAME.source A vSphere port group. Every NIC of every member must be on a mapped port group networks.NAME.type public: the instance's public interface, DHCP. private: an Exoscale managed private network networks.NAME.cidr The subnet of a private network. The top host address (.254 of a /24) belongs to Exoscale's DHCP server: a VM using it must be renumbered networks.NAME.exoscale_name An existing private network to use instead of creating v2v-GROUP-NAME (the appliance role only attaches v2v-* networks) vms[].tier 1 = back end. Members of a tier stop and start together vms[].ip {NETWORK: ADDRESS} when VMware Tools do not report the address vms[].security_groups Attached at cutover. Existing groups, or ones defined under security_groups: vms[].health tcp: PORT, http: URL (2xx/3xx, optional expect: TEXT in the body), command: SHELL (exit 0), timeout vms[].name The instance's final name, applied by group cleanup vms[] other keys As the plan options: instance_type, system_disk, receiver_template, receiver_template_visibility, fold, no_fold

Placeholders in health checks and hooks: {public_ip}, {private_ip}, {ip.NETWORK} (the member's own), and {VM.public_ip}, {VM.private_ip}, {VM.ip.NETWORK} for any member. Hooks also get V2V_GROUP, V2V_STEP and V2V_<VM>_PUBLIC_IP / V2V_<VM>_PRIVATE_IP in their environment, and run in the manifest's directory.

docs.title: Networks
docs.text:
Each Exoscale instance gets its public interface first, then one NIC per private network, in the order of the source NICs. group create attaches the private networks to the receivers, each address as a static lease, so their MAC addresses are known before the cutover. The conversion then writes a map into the guest (/etc/v2v-netfix.map) that the first-boot network fix follows:

Source NIC On Exoscale On a public port group (DHCP) The public interface, DHCP Static address on a private port group The private network NIC with the same address. Its gateway is removed: there is no router on a private network, so the default route goes through the public interface Only private NICs (a typical database) The same, plus a DHCP configuration for the public interface

The fix works on ifupdown, netplan, NetworkManager keyfiles and ifcfg files, whatever the interface names were on VMware (ens192, eth0...). Windows gets its addresses from a first-boot task that matches the new adapters by MAC.

Every member keeps a public IP. Its security groups decide what reaches it: with v2v-shop-closed above, nothing does except the appliance, which the migration's own exo-v2v-<member> group lets in (SSH and the health check ports) until cleanup. Traffic between members on a private network is not filtered by security groups.

The load balancer's public IP is its receiver's IP, known from group create on, so DNS can be prepared before the window. Elastic IPs are not handled (they need configuration in the guest).

Static DNS servers in the guests' configurations are kept. If they are on premises, change them before the cutover or in the post_cutover hook.

docs.title: The cutover
docs.text:
1. Preflight: every member synced within max_sync_age, its receiver running and attached to its private networks, no blocking problem in the preflight reports, no other command running on it.
  2. Last warm cycle on every member in parallel, to make the final copies small.
  3. pre_cutover hook. Nothing is stopped before this point: a failure here leaves the application running on VMware.
  4. Stop, front to back. The members of the highest tier shut down; each member's final copy and conversion start as soon as it is off. When the whole tier is off, the next one shuts down.
  5. Conversions run in parallel, each on its own instance, with the volume rebuilds that some filesystems need.
  6. Instances stopped and resized to their final types.
  7. Start, back to front. Tier 1 starts and its health checks must pass, then tier 2, and so on.
  8. post_cutover hook, then the report: the window and each member's downtime.

If a step fails, the cutover stops there and prints the state. The members that were converting finish first, so each one stops in a consistent state. Then either fix the problem and run group cutover again, which resumes, or run group rollback. With rollback_on_failure: true, or when max_window is exceeded with it, the rollback starts by itself.

The VMs are shut down cleanly in order, so the database stops after the applications that write to it and each disk is consistent: no snapshot across VMs is needed.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
group rollback stops the Exoscale instances, front first, then powers the sources on, back end first, waiting for VMware Tools in each tier before the next one. Members whose conversion had not started keep their receivers: group sync continues from their last cycle. Converted members must be created again for another attempt: group cleanup shop --delete-instances, then group plan, create and sync.

Data written on Exoscale after the cutover is not copied back.

docs.title: Clean-up
docs.text:
After you validated the application, group cleanup removes each member's exo-v2v-<member> security group and rollback volumes, and renames the instances to their name. The private networks, anti-affinity groups and security groups stay: the migrated instances use them.

group cleanup --delete-instances abandons the move: it deletes the instances and volumes (--force for members already cut over), then the networks, groups and security groups group create made.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One appliance replicates every member: it must see all their datastores.
  • Members are listed by name (--vm); selecting by vCenter folder or tag comes later.
  • One zone per group.
  • Managed private networks only (no VPC subnets yet); no Elastic IPs.
  • No rehearsal (a test cutover on copies while the sources keep running) yet.

docs.title: IAM role for the replication appliance
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.3.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

The replication appliance calls the Exoscale API through the exo CLI. Give it an API key bound to a dedicated role, not your account's own key.

exo-v2v only uses the Compute service: instances, Block Storage volumes, security groups and, for groups, private networks and anti-affinity groups. Everything it creates follows fixed naming rules, which the role below uses to limit what the key can touch.

Resource Name Target instance v2v-<migration> (group members: v2v-<group>-<vm>) Block Storage volumes v2v-<migration>-d<N>, v2v-<migration>-d<N>-4k Security group of a migration exo-v2v-<migration> Temporary SSH key (registered by exo while it creates the instance, then deleted) v2v-<migration>-<timestamp> Group private network v2v-<group>-<network> (or a v2v-* network you name with exoscale_name) Group anti-affinity group v2v-<group>-<name> Security groups a group manifest defines v2v-* (or exo-v2v-*)

If you name the instance yourself with create --instance-name, start the name with v2v-, or the role below refuses it.

exo-v2v also labels its instances and volumes exo-v2v=<migration>, but the role does not rely on labels: in our tests, Exoscale IAM refused create-instance and create-block-storage-volume calls under a rule that checked parameters.labels, while rules on names worked.

docs.title: The role
docs.text:
iam/exo-v2v-appliance-policy.json:

Rule Allows 1 Every read operation (get-*, list-*) in Compute: zones, templates, instance types, and the state of the resources above 2 Creating v2v-* instances, volumes, SSH keys, private networks and anti-affinity groups 3 Deleting v2v-* SSH keys 4 Starting, stopping, scaling, resetting, renaming (update-instance, used by cleanup for a group member's final name) and deleting v2v-* instances. Reset: when the source system disk grows during replication, the target is re-imaged with a bigger root disk 5 Attaching a v2v-* volume to a v2v-* instance 6 Detaching, relabelling, resizing and deleting v2v-* volumes 7 Attaching instances to v2v-* private networks (with a static lease) 8 Deleting v2v-* private networks 9 Deleting v2v-* anti-affinity groups 10 Creating exo-v2v-* and v2v-* security groups 11 Adding rules to, deleting, and detaching instances from exo-v2v-* and v2v-* security groups 12 Attaching an instance to a security group (cutover attaches the groups you name in plan --security-group or in a group manifest)

Everything else is denied, including every other Exoscale service. The operations in the rules are the ones exo-v2v calls through exo 1.103: recorded during a full migration with 0.1.0 (create, sync, cutover with a volume rebuild, cleanup), plus the security-group attach and detach used by plan --security-group and by cleanup without --delete-instance. 0.2.0 adds resize-block-storage-volume (a data disk that grows during replication) and reset-instance (a system disk that grows). 0.3.0 adds what groups need: create-private-network, attach-instance-to-private-network, delete-private-network, create-anti-affinity-group, delete-anti-affinity-group, update-instance (rename), and v2v-* security groups. Exoscale evaluates attach-instance-to-private-network against the private network, not the instance: a rule on the instance name never matches it.

To update an existing role: exo iam role update exo-v2v-appliance --policy - < docs/iam/exo-v2v-appliance-policy.json.

Create the role and a key bound to it with the exo CLI, from an account that can manage IAM:

exo iam role create exo-v2v-appliance \
  --description "exo-v2v replication appliance" \
  --policy - < docs/iam/exo-v2v-appliance-policy.json
exo iam api-key create exo-v2v-appliance exo-v2v-appliance

The second command prints the key and its secret once. On the appliance, store them with exo config or export them as EXOSCALE_API_KEY and EXOSCALE_API_SECRET for the user that runs exo-v2v.

docs.title: Check the role before production
docs.text:
We validated this role on 2026-10-19 with two complete migrations (Ubuntu 24.04, and AlmaLinux 9 with a volume rebuild) through cleanup --delete-instance, on 2026-10-21 with a data disk and a system disk that grew during replication, and on 2026-10-23 with three group runs (5 VMs): group create (private network, anti-affinity group, security groups, receivers attached to the private network with static leases), the cutovers, group rollback, group cleanup --delete-instances, and a hand-over group cleanup with a rename. Every exo call was made with the role's key.

Run one migration of a small test VM with your new key too, through cleanup --delete-instance. A refused call stops exo-v2v with an error that names the exo command; check the Exoscale console for leftovers after a failed test.

docs.title: What the role does not restrict
docs.text:
• Read operations cover every Compute resource of the organization, not only exo-v2v's: the exo CLI looks resources up by name.
  • Rule 9 lets the key attach any security group to any instance. Exoscale evaluates that operation against the security group, not the instance.
  • Every rule matches names (v2v-, exo-v2v-), not labels. Do not give other instances, volumes, SSH keys, private networks, anti-affinity groups or security groups names with those prefixes, or the key can manage them too.
  • Rule 7 lets the key attach any v2v-* instance to a v2v-* private network.
  • A group member renamed at cleanup leaves the role's scope: that is the hand-over (the key can no longer stop or delete it).

docs.title: A simpler alternative
docs.text:
If you prefer a role that is easier to read, allow the whole Compute service and nothing else:

{
  "default-service-strategy": "deny",
  "services": { "compute": { "type": "allow", "rules": [] } }
}

It can manage every Compute resource of the organization, so use it only in an organization dedicated to the migration.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.3.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

Known limits of exo-v2v 0.3.0. exo-v2v plan reports the ones it can detect before anything is created.

docs.title: Source VM
docs.text: Limit Details At most 5 data disks as volumes An Exoscale instance attaches up to 5 Block Storage volumes next to its root disk. Disks carried inside the root disk (--fold, automatic for a disk that shares a filesystem with the system disk) do not count. A volume rebuild at cutover needs a free slot per rebuilt volume. System disk Found from the boot order or VMware Tools; plan warns when it had to guess (run it with the VM on and Tools running, or pass --system-disk) Snapshot chains Supported. A revert to a snapshot during replication makes the next cycle a full copy of the allocated areas Disk changes during replication A grown disk is followed (volume resized; a grown system disk resets the target instance, whose root disk is then copied again), a new disk gets a new volume, a removed disk stops sync Windows dynamic disks and Storage Spaces Not supported on data disks: their metadata counts 512-byte sectors. The disks are detected and left untouched; their volumes stay unreadable on Exoscale. Convert them to basic disks first (a spanned or striped volume must be copied to a basic volume). plan warns when VMware Tools show a volume spread over several disks. No independent disks or RDMs Independent disks are left out of snapshots, so changes cannot be tracked. Raw device mappings are not VMDK files. Root disk of 10 GB or more Smaller disks are rounded up to 10 GB Disk sizes rounded up Each disk becomes the next whole GB; volumes get at least 1 MiB extra Network interfaces A single migration gets one public interface (DHCP). In a group, each port group maps to the public interface or a managed private network, and the guest's configuration follows. Static IP addresses In a group, a static address on a private port group is kept on the Exoscale private network. Otherwise the guest keeps its old static configuration: switch it to DHCP before the cutover, or update it on the instance. Secure Boot and vTPM Carried over: the instance is created with Secure Boot and a TPM when the source has them (Exoscale sets both at creation). Secrets sealed to the VMware vTPM do not move. Secure Boot is tested; the TPM is not. A guest that only boots because Secure Boot is off at the source cannot gain it later: Exoscale cannot turn it on after creation. Encrypted disks and encrypted VMs Not supported (LUKS, BitLocker, vSphere VM encryption)

docs.title: Block Storage sector size
docs.text:
Exoscale Block Storage volumes use 4096-byte sectors; VMware disks use 512. exo-v2v adapts data volumes at cutover, with these limits:

Case Behaviour Partition tables (GPT, MBR) Rewritten in place. Partitions must start on a 4 KiB boundary, which is the default for every current installer. NTFS (Windows) Adapted in place, no data moved. The volume must use clusters of 4 KiB or more (the default). XFS created with 512-byte sectors (RHEL-family default on VMware), ext with 1 KiB blocks Rebuilt on a new volume with the same identifiers. The cutover takes longer in proportion to the data on these volumes. The original volume is kept, detached, as a rollback copy until cleanup --delete-rollback-volumes. The same filesystems inside LVM logical volumes Rebuilt the same way, logical volume by logical volume. A volume group spread over several volumes is rebuilt across as many new volumes, keeping the PV, VG and LV identifiers. Linear and striped logical volumes only: thin, RAID, mirror, cache and snapshot logical volumes with such a filesystem are reported, not rebuilt. A volume group that spans the system disk and other disks Those disks are carried inside the root disk (512-byte sectors), so nothing is rebuilt. Detected by plan through VMware Tools; otherwise the preflight at the first sync reports it: plan again with --fold DISK. Root disk Not affected: the instance's root disk uses 512-byte sectors

docs.title: Replication
docs.text: Limit Details The appliance must run in the source vSphere It reads snapshot disks by attaching them to itself, so it must be on a host that sees the VM's datastores. Copy speed Limited by the datastore and the appliance's CPU. In our lab (HDD datastore, 2 vCPU appliance) a full copy ran at about 30 MiB/s per VM. Later cycles copy only changes. Snapshot per cycle Each cycle creates and removes a snapshot, which briefly pauses the VM, as backups do Target instance restarts during replication The target instance runs its agent from memory. If it restarts before the cutover, it boots a partly copied disk: run cleanup --delete-instance, then create and sync again (a full copy). Instance type during replication The target instance runs as standard.large or larger until the cutover, then is scaled to its final type Datastore types Tested on VMFS. vSAN and vVols are untested.

docs.title: Cutover and after
docs.text: Limit Details Downtime Shutdown, last delta, conversion (2–5 min) and boot: 2 to 9 minutes in our tests, longer if a volume must be rebuilt Rollback exo-v2v rollback powers the source VM back on. Data written on Exoscale after the cutover is not copied back. Windows first boot Windows finishes installing drivers for a few minutes after RDP opens and may reboot. Data disks come online when it finishes. Windows licensing Contact Exoscale before migrating Windows workloads (see Supported operating systems) Zones Tested in ch-gva-2. Conversion needs nested virtualization on the instance type.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: Limit Details One appliance per group It replicates every member, so it must see all their datastores Members by name group discover --vm; selecting by vCenter folder or tag is not available yet One zone Every member of a group goes to the same zone Private networks Managed private networks only (no VPC subnets). The top host address of the subnet (.254 of a /24) belongs to Exoscale's DHCP server: a VM using it must be renumbered. The appliance role only attaches v2v-* private networks Default route Moves to the public interface: a private network has no router. Routes to other networks through the old gateway are lost DNS servers Static DNS servers in the guests' configurations are kept; change on-premises ones before or during the cutover (post_cutover hook) Elastic IPs Not handled: the load balancer keeps its instance's public IP, known from group create on Health checks Run from the appliance against the members' public IPs (the ports are opened to the appliance only) Rehearsal No test cutover on copies yet Rollback after conversion Converted members must be created again before another attempt (a full copy)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.3.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

Check these before your first migration. exo-v2v plan checks the source VM for you and refuses VMs it cannot migrate.

docs.title: vSphere
docs.text:
Item Requirement Version vCenter Server or standalone ESXi, 6.7 or later. Tested on ESXi 7.0 Update 3. Account A vSphere account with the privileges below, passed to exo-v2v as VSPHERE_HOST, VSPHERE_USER and VSPHERE_PASSWORD Datastore space Room for a short-lived snapshot of each VM during each sync cycle (the changes written while a cycle runs)

Privileges for the migration account:

On Privileges Source VMs VirtualMachine.State.CreateSnapshot, VirtualMachine.State.RemoveSnapshot, VirtualMachine.Config.ChangeTracking, VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOff, VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOn, VirtualMachine.Provisioning.DiskRandomRead Replication appliance VM VirtualMachine.Config.AddExistingDisk, VirtualMachine.Config.RemoveDisk Datastores of the source VMs Datastore.FileManagement (read)

docs.title: Replication appliance
docs.text:
The appliance is a Linux VM that runs exo-v2v. It must run inside the same vSphere environment as the VMs you migrate, on a host that can see their datastores: exo-v2v attaches the frozen snapshot disks to it read-only. One appliance can serve many migrations.

Item Requirement Operating system Ubuntu 24.04 or Debian 12 or later (any Linux with Python 3.10+ works) Size 2 vCPU, 4 GiB RAM, 20 GB disk. Copy throughput is limited by the appliance's CPU; give it 4 vCPU for several migrations in parallel. SCSI controller A VMware Paravirtual (pvscsi) controller with free slots, used to attach the snapshot disks. Add a second one if you run many migrations at once. Software Python 3.10 or later, ssh, the exo CLI 1.102 or later, and exo-v2v (pip install exo_v2v-*.whl) Privileges sync, cutover and rollback read block devices and must run as root (sudo -E keeps the environment variables)

Network access from the appliance:

Destination Port Why vCenter or ESXi TCP 443 vSphere API Exoscale API (api-<zone>.exoscale.com) TCP 443 Create and manage the target instance Target instances in the Exoscale zone TCP 22 Data stream and agent control, inside SSH api.ipify.org or ifconfig.me TCP 443 Detects the appliance's public address once per migration. Not needed if you pass create --sender-cidr. Group members' public IPs (groups only) the health check ports group cutover checks each tier from the appliance; the member's own security group opens those ports to the appliance only

The appliance's public address must stay the same during a migration: the migration's security group admits SSH from that address only.

The web status page listens on the appliance's loopback interface by default; reach it through an SSH port forward.

docs.title: Exoscale
docs.text: Item Requirement Account An organization with quota for the instance types you target, Block Storage volumes and one security group per running migration; for a group, one private network per private port group and every member's receiver at once API key A key restricted to the Compute service, configured in the exo CLI (exo config) or in EXOSCALE_API_KEY and EXOSCALE_API_SECRET. See IAM role for a ready-made role. Instance type during migration Conversion needs at least 8 GiB of RAM and nested virtualization, so the target instance runs as standard.large (or larger) until cutover, then is scaled to its final type. Tested in ch-gva-2. Internet access from the target instance Not needed with a receiver template. Without one, the target instance installs packages from Debian or Ubuntu mirrors, and for Windows guests downloads the virtio drivers from fedorapeople.org.

docs.title: Source VM
docs.text: Item Requirement Operating system See Supported operating systems Disks At most 6 virtual disks (1 root disk and up to 5 Block Storage volumes). No independent disks, no raw device mappings (RDM). Firmware BIOS or UEFI. The target instance uses the same boot mode, and Secure Boot and a TPM when the source has them. Changed Block Tracking Enabled automatically by exo-v2v, without downtime VMware Tools Recommended, running when you run plan: it tells exo-v2v which disk holds the system and which disks share a filesystem with it. At cutover it shuts the guest down cleanly; without it, exo-v2v powers the VM off after --shutdown-timeout. Network configuration For a single migration, DHCP is recommended: a static IP configuration keeps the old address and must be updated for the Exoscale instance's address. In a group, static addresses on private port groups are kept on Exoscale private networks. Snapshots Existing snapshots are allowed but consolidate them first if you can

docs.title: Receiver templates
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.3.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

A receiver template is an Exoscale template that boots straight into the exo-v2v receiver: a Linux system that runs entirely from RAM, so the migration can overwrite the instance's own disk. With a receiver template, exo-v2v create takes about one minute instead of 5 to 15, and the target instance needs no access to package mirrors.

Without one, create starts the target instance from a stock Linux template, installs the conversion tools on it and switches it into RAM (kexec). Both ways produce the same receiver; the rest of the migration is identical.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
Exoscale does not publish receiver templates yet: build and register your own (below). Exoscale-published Windows variants would carry the Windows licence, so a migrated Windows guest would run on a Windows-licensed instance. Until then, contact Exoscale about licensing before migrating Windows guests.

Templates built before exo-v2v 0.2.0 lack dmsetup, which 0.2.0 uses to rebuild LVM logical volumes. Such a receiver installs it when it needs it, which requires access to a package mirror: rebuild your templates to avoid that.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
The template's boot mode must match the VM's firmware. One image boots in both modes, with or without Secure Boot (Canonical-signed shim, GRUB and kernel), so Secure Boot is chosen per instance, not per template.

Template Boot mode For exo-v2v-linux-uefi UEFI Linux VMs with UEFI firmware exo-v2v-linux-legacy legacy Linux VMs with BIOS firmware exo-v2v-windows-uefi UEFI Windows VMs with UEFI firmware exo-v2v-windows-legacy legacy Windows VMs with BIOS firmware

The Windows variants also carry the virtio-win drivers and rhsrvany that virt-v2v needs to convert Windows guests. A Windows VM with BIOS firmware keeps BIOS on Exoscale: no conversion to UEFI is needed.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
exo-v2v plan web01 --vm web01 --zone ch-gva-2 \
  --receiver-template exo-v2v-linux-uefi [--receiver-template-visibility private]
exo-v2v create web01

plan refuses a template whose boot mode does not match the VM. The receiver logs in as v2v; exo-v2v handles that.

docs.title: Build and register
docs.text:
template/receiver.pkr.hcl builds the image and registers both boot-mode variants with Exoscale's Packer plugin. Run it on Ubuntu 24.04, as a user with passwordless sudo, with an Exoscale API key that can register templates and write to an existing Object Storage bucket:

sudo apt-get install -y mmdebstrap qemu-utils gdisk dosfstools grub-pc-bin grub-efi-amd64-signed shim-signed
export EXOSCALE_API_KEY=EXO… EXOSCALE_API_SECRET=…
packer init template/
packer build -var flavour=linux   -var image_bucket=BUCKET template/   # exo-v2v-linux-uefi, -legacy
packer build -var flavour=windows -var image_bucket=BUCKET template/   # exo-v2v-windows-uefi, -legacy
Variable Default Meaning flavour linux linux, or windows (adds virtio-win and rhsrvany) image_bucket Existing bucket in the first zone; the image is removed after import zones ["ch-gva-2"] Zones to register the templates in (templates are per zone) template_prefix exo-v2v Template names: <prefix>-<flavour>-uefi and -legacy

The recipe runs template/build-image.sh, which you can also run by hand and register yourself:

sudo template/build-image.sh linux exo-v2v-linux.qcow2       # ~230 MB; windows: ~600 MB
exo storage upload exo-v2v-linux.qcow2 sos://BUCKET/
URL=$(exo storage presign sos://BUCKET/exo-v2v-linux.qcow2 -e 1h)
for m in uefi legacy; do
  exo compute instance-template register exo-v2v-linux-$m "$URL" "$(md5sum < exo-v2v-linux.qcow2 | cut -d' ' -f1)" \
    --zone ch-gva-2 --boot-mode $m --username v2v --disable-password
done

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The image is a 10 GB disk with a BIOS boot partition and an EFI system partition. GRUB loads the kernel and a ~220 MB initramfs that holds the whole receiver system (virt-v2v, libguestfs, QEMU, filesystem tools). The disk is never mounted.
  • At boot the receiver reads the migration's SSH key from the instance user-data, generates its own SSH host keys and starts SSH. The Windows variant first copies virtio-win from the EFI partition into RAM.
  • create waits for SSH before attaching the Block Storage volumes, then streams the exo-v2v agent over SSH and starts it.

docs.title: Supported operating systems
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.3.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

exo-v2v converts guests with virt-v2v-in-place, so it can migrate the guests virt-v2v supports. The tables below separate what we tested end to end from what we expect to work.

docs.title: Tested
docs.text:
Each guest below was migrated live from ESXi 7.0 Update 3 to Exoscale (zone ch-gva-2) while running, with a system disk and a separate data disk. After each migration we compared marker files on both disks with their checksums from the VMware build, and checked the boot, the network, the mounted data disk and the services.

Operating system BIOS UEFI Data disk Downtime Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Yes Yes Not checked: the test image's data disk was blank 2–3 min Debian 13 Yes Yes ext4 4–5 min AlmaLinux 9.8, SELinux enforcing Yes Yes XFS created with 512-byte sectors (rebuilt for 4 KiB sectors at cutover) 5–7 min Windows Server 2022 Yes Yes NTFS (adapted to 4 KiB sectors in place) 5–8 min Windows Server 2025 Yes Yes NTFS (adapted to 4 KiB sectors in place) 6–9 min

The downtime column covers every run. The chart shows the final run of each guest through a receiver template:

Ubuntu 24.04 and Windows Server 2022 were also migrated from UEFI with Secure Boot on: both booted on Exoscale with Secure Boot on (downtime 133 s and 455 s).

A Debian 13 VM under continuous write load was also migrated with a downtime of 5 minutes and no lost writes. Up to 8 migrations ran at the same time from one replication appliance. Every guest above was migrated with a receiver template; all except Windows Server 2025 also without one.

docs.title: Multi-disk VMs, LVM and VMDK chains
docs.text:
Two AlmaLinux 9 VMs (SELinux enforcing, XFS with 512-byte sectors, the RHEL default on VMware) were migrated live with cutover --verify (every disk hash-compared before conversion):

VM What it had Result 4 disks on 3 controllers (2 paravirtual SCSI, NVMe) Root volume group on the system disk; XFS data disk; a volume group over a GPT partition of one disk and the whole NVMe disk, with an XFS logical volume spanning both and an ext4 one Pass: the XFS data disk and the spanning logical volume rebuilt with 4 KiB sectors (across two new volumes, same LVM and filesystem UUIDs), every file intact Root volume group extended onto a second disk, data disk grown before the migration Replication through a 3-level snapshot chain, then between cycles: a middle snapshot deleted, a revert to a snapshot, the data disk grown, the system disk grown, a disk hot-added Pass: the second disk carried inside the root disk; the revert copied the allocated areas again (the reverted file is absent, the later ones present); the data volume resized; the receiver reset with a bigger root disk; a volume added for the new disk

docs.title: An application moved as a group
docs.text:
A 5-VM application was moved with exo-v2v group (tiers, private network with the VMs' static addresses, health checks), three times:

VM Guest Network configuration on VMware Result Load balancer Debian 13, HAProxy ifupdown, a DHCP front NIC and a static back NIC Front NIC on the public interface, back NIC on the private network with its address 2 application servers AlmaLinux 9 (NetworkManager, eth0 naming), Ubuntu 24.04 (netplan) Static address, default route via the on-premises gateway Address kept on the private network, default route moved to the public interface Database AlmaLinux 9, PostgreSQL on an XFS data disk with 512-byte sectors Static address Same; data disk rebuilt for 4 KiB sectors, every row present Windows member Windows Server 2022 Static address Address set on the private network adapter at first boot

Window (first VM stopped to last tier healthy): 461 s for 4 VMs, 486 s for 5. A conversion failure injected on one member stopped the group, and group rollback brought the application back on VMware without losing data.

A Windows Server 2022 VM with a spanned dynamic volume over two disks lost that volume on Exoscale, as expected (see Limitations); its basic C: and D: volumes migrated fine. exo-v2v now reports dynamic disks before the cutover.

docs.title: Expected to work
docs.text:
These are supported by virt-v2v and use the same mechanisms as the tested guests, but we have not migrated them in our lab. Migrate a non-critical VM first.

Family Versions Red Hat Enterprise Linux and rebuilds (Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, CentOS Stream) 8, 9, 10 Debian 11, 12 Ubuntu LTS 20.04, 22.04 SUSE Linux Enterprise Server, openSUSE Leap 15 Windows Server 2016, 2019

Older releases (for example RHEL 7 or Windows Server 2012 R2) may convert but are out of their vendors' support; we do not recommend them.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text: Case Why Windows client editions (Windows 10, 11) Not tested; out of scope for this release Encrypted system disks (LUKS, BitLocker) The conversion has to read and modify the guest's system disk Operating systems other than Linux and Windows (FreeBSD, Solaris, …) virt-v2v does not convert them 32-bit guests Not tested; Exoscale instances are 64-bit VMs with more than 5 data disks (unless carried inside the root disk), independent disks or raw device mappings See Limitations Windows dynamic disks and Storage Spaces as data disks Their metadata counts 512-byte sectors; see Limitations

docs.title: Windows licensing
docs.text: A migrated Windows Server runs on an instance created from a Linux template, unless its receiver template is a Windows-licensed one published by Exoscale (not available yet, see Receiver templates). Contact Exoscale before migrating Windows workloads to agree on licensing.

docs.title: Web status page
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.3.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

exo-v2v web serves a read-only page with the state of every migration and group on the replication appliance: phases, the last cycles, cutover steps, downtime, member logs. Share it with the people who follow a migration without giving them a shell.

sudo -E exo-v2v web                      # http://127.0.0.1:8780/

Run it as the user that runs the migrations (sudo -E, the same EXO_V2V_HOME): it reads their state files.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
Page Content Overview Groups (cutover state, members by tier and phase), every migration: phase, a sync or cutover running now, last cycle, public and private addresses, downtime Migration Phase, source VM, receiver, a chart of the data copied per cycle (full, delta, final), disks and where they go, networks with the Exoscale MACs, the cutover steps with their times, plan and preflight messages, events Group Members by tier with their health check results, the cutover steps (preflight, warm cycle, tiers off, conversions, tiers up, hooks) with their times, networks, a member's log, events

The page refreshes every 5 seconds. It needs no internet access: no external scripts, fonts or images.

docs.title: Read-only
docs.text:
• Only GET and HEAD; any other method gets 405.
  • It never writes a file and never takes a lock: a running sync or cutover is found from the process ID its lock file records.
  • It needs no Exoscale or vSphere credentials, and serves no keys: the migration's SSH key and the tunnel's known_hosts are not exposed. Logs are served only for group members, by name.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
It listens on 127.0.0.1:8780 by default. From your workstation:

ssh -L 8780:127.0.0.1:8780 appliance      # then open http://127.0.0.1:8780/

To listen on another address, set a token; the page refuses to start without one:

openssl rand -hex 24 | sudo tee /etc/exo-v2v-web.token >/dev/null
sudo -E exo-v2v web --listen 0.0.0.0:8780 --token-file /etc/exo-v2v-web.token

Open http://appliance:8780/login?token=TOKEN once: it sets an HTTP-only cookie. API clients send Authorization: Bearer TOKEN. The page is plain HTTP: put it behind a TLS reverse proxy, or keep the SSH tunnel, on any network you do not trust. EXO_V2V_WEB_TOKEN can carry the token instead of a file.

docs.title: Run it as a service
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/exo-v2v-web.service
[Unit]
Description=exo-v2v read-only status page
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Environment=EXO_V2V_HOME=/var/lib/exo-v2v
ExecStart=/opt/exo-v2v/bin/exo-v2v web --listen 127.0.0.1:8780
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

docs.title: JSON API
docs.text: Path Returns /api/overview Host, version, groups and migrations (summaries) /api/migrations/NAME One migration: plan, cycles, cutover steps, events /api/groups/NAME One group: members, cutover, networks, events /api/groups/NAME/log/VM?lines=N The last N lines (at most 2000) of a member's log
